A printed claim can be examined—but not perfectly recovered.

ACT 03 / THE VISUAL ARGUMENT

A graphic becomes a way of thinking.

Scroll through five visual arguments. The same source observations remain underneath every scene. At any point, enter the full interactive laboratory to inspect or challenge the evidence.

01 / THE MASTERPIECE

First, see the whole.

Minard's 1869 map assembles several dimensions of a campaign into one coherent visual argument. The width of the moving band is not decoration—it represents estimated men present.

What do you understand before reading a single number?

02 / SEEING QUANTITY

A shrinking width. An enormous change.

The main advance is recorded at 340,000 at its first source location and 100,000 near Moscow. The wider starting figure of 422,000 combines three initially represented formations. These are different denominators.

The design is powerful because the quantity becomes visible, not because a caption tells us what to believe.

03 / THE MISSING EXPLANATION

Much of the change precedes the retreat.

Follow the main advance toward Moscow. The ribbon narrows considerably before the temperatures plotted below the retreat. A familiar winter-only explanation cannot be read straight off the picture.

Change in men present is not automatically a death count; the chart does not assign causes.

04 / A CRITICAL DISTINCTION

Time appears—but not everywhere.

Nine temperature values are transcribed; eight have calendar dates. The 51 troop records have locations and an order, but no dates for each row. We can reconstruct their spatial sequence, not an observed daily force series.

Motion helps tell a story. It cannot manufacture observations.

05 / THE ANALYTICAL TURN

A pattern is not a proof of cause.

Extreme cold, falling numbers and geography share a visual frame. That permits meaningful questions. Explaining *how many* men were lost to weather, combat, supply failure or disease requires independent evidence.

Our job is to distinguish observation, inference and claim.

ARCHIVAL FIDELITY · RECONSTRUCTION AUDIT

Faithful to the data. Not a facsimile.

Minard's 1869 plate represents numbers through ribbon width, identifies advance and retreat, and connects temperature to geography. Our live coordinate map preserves these relationships, but the published transcription does not encode every bend, annotation, or graphic adjustment of the lithograph.

HISTORICAL FIDELITY / ORIGINAL VS RECONSTRUCTION

The artifact remains the reference.

Our live graphics use published longitude, latitude and troop observations. They preserve the data encoding and main branching logic, but cannot claim to reproduce every curve, annotation or artistic choice in the 1869 printed sheet. V12 bundles the supplied original scan and a separate image-derived ribbon silhouette, with an adjustable measured-but-provisional archival alignment and preserves the source-row transformation and a structured fidelity audit, not an archival facsimile.

THE CLOSING ARGUMENT / WHAT WE SHOULD CARRY FORWARD

A beautiful graphic invites belief. A rigorous one invites inspection.

Minard's achievement was to encode several relationships in one coherent image. Our responsibility as readers is to keep the observation distinct from the explanation.

01 / ENCODING

Make magnitude visible.

Ribbon width means quantity. If the proportions are distorted, the argument changes with them.

Examine the encoding ↗
02 / COMPARISON

Keep the denominator honest.

Different formations, stages and estimates cannot be merged into a single death count.

Compare the observations ↗
03 / INFERENCE

Do not confuse pattern with cause.

Weather, geography and loss of strength appear together; attribution needs more evidence.

Challenge the claim ↗
The standard: show the evidence, reveal the design, and leave room to question the conclusion.Inspect methods and sources →
PUBLICATION RECORD / THE EVIDENCE CONTRACT

What the graphic knows—and what it does not.

Every interpretation rests on three distinct objects: Minard's original image, later transcription of plotted values, and this project's interactive reconstruction. These must never be mistaken for interchangeable historical records.

01 / ORIGINAL ARTIFACT

Preserved visual evidence

The supplied 2003 × 955 historical image is included in this release. The separate gold-and-black isolation layer is derived from its pixels, not itself a historical document.

Inspect the original ↗
02 / MEASURED TRANSCRIPTION

Observations with limits

51 troop records and 20 mapped places provide geography and estimated quantities. Nine temperatures are recorded, but only eight have an associated calendar date. None of the troop rows contains a daily date.

Examine the evidence ↗
03 / INTERPRETIVE RECONSTRUCTION

Approximate alignment

Our geographic SVG and affine calibration are independently computed from transcribed observations and manually selected image landmarks. The registered coordinates are provisional, not an archival-grade tracing.

Examine the reconstruction ↗

What visitors may reasonably conclude

Magnitude, place, direction and the dated cold observations can be compared visually. The changing width reflects estimated men present within reported formations. The reader can observe declines before the recorded coldest period.

What the visualization cannot prove

The recorded difference between two force estimates is not automatically the number of people who died. The chart cannot apportion deaths to weather, battle, disease or logistics, and an animated transition cannot invent the dates missing from troop observations.

Inspect or export the underlying observations

These accessible tables are part of the HTML itself. They work without interaction scripts and allow readers to verify plotted values independently of colour or shape.

SOURCES · METHODS · LIMITS

Every mark has an origin.

Data-backed reconstruction from the HistData transcription of Minard’s 1869 graphic (51 troop observations, 20 places, nine temperature values). V12 integrates the guided visual essay, bundles the supplied archival image and an image-derived ribbon silhouette, and preserves quantitative transformation, synchronized trace and reconstruction audit. This is not a facsimile of the hand-drawn lithograph, a military census, or a day-by-day force simulation.

Important: HistData's help text contains an apparent 1815 date error for this campaign. We use 1812, and leave the temperature record with the missing date explicitly undated.
